data.title: Why Did A Coherent (COHR) Director Triple Their Stake?
data.description:
• Independent director Stephen Pagliuca bought $34.7m of Coherent (NYSE:COHR) stock on November 24, 2026, increasing his holding to roughly three times its previous size.
  • Over twelve months, three insiders bought and six insiders sold, with trading tilting towards the buyers.

Coherent’s recent insider activity shows directors committing additional personal capital to the business. For investors who want to see where other corporate leaders are also buying shares with their own money, it is worth reviewing 70 undervalued small caps that insiders are buying.

Coherent insiders are pulling in different directions

Stephen Pagliuca has been the clear outlier at Coherent, committing fresh capital while several board colleagues have been trimming their exposure. Independent Non-Employee Directors Joseph Corasanti and Enrico Digirolamo both reduced their holdings over the past year, with Corasanti cutting his stake by 16% and Digirolamo reducing his by 27% across a run of sales. The shares now trade 33% below Digirolamo's average sale price, a drop that person avoided on the stock sold, while Corasanti's trades line up with a price that is close to where the shares change hands today.

Pagliuca's activity has gone the other way. The November 2026 purchase followed earnings early that month that set out how the business had been trading, and the shares have since stayed close to the level where Pagliuca and the other buyers paid in. The November move was also the second open market purchase from Pagliuca in a year, so it reads more as a run of buying than a one off. Taken together, these filings show non-employee directors split between one heavyweight buyer and a couple of measured sellers. This points more to mixed conviction than a clear shared signal.

AI optics demand has to translate into durable high margin Coherent revenue

For Stephen Pagliuca’s November 24, 2026 buying to work, Coherent needs its AI optics push to show up in sustained high margin business rather than a short spike. The November 19, 2026 repurchase plan points to the board committing capital at roughly the same price, and the stock sitting around the insiders’ levels means that test is still open.

Coherent now needs AI datacenter and high performance computing buildouts to keep pulling in record Datacenter & Communications orders with long visibility. Internal manufacturing projects, including extra indium phosphide lines, have to deliver scale and a leaner cost base that supports better profitability. PhotonLink and higher value datacenter interconnect products then need to ramp on those contracts so revenue mix supports the margin targets set out in COHR: AI Optics Demand Was The Hook, Order Visibility And Margins Drive The Case.

Insider trades sit on a typical base

Several insiders bought Coherent shares with their own money, and the register shows how much of the company they share in. Insiders together hold 0.3% of the company, worth $126.6m at today’s price, which is typical for a company this size. Their trades come from people with a material personal exposure, but not from owners who control where most of the equity sits.

Insiders’ buying and selling at Coherent reflects meaningful personal positioning, but it does not appear to be the kind of activity that reshapes who really owns the stock.
